name: Euphorbia

project_scope.note: All 12 current Euphorbia concepts are already canonical learner taxa. Range labels remain independent from learner inclusion.

taxonomy_notes.legacy_mapping: Several small sandmat species entered the source pool under Chamaesyce; their canonical learner cards retain those names as synonyms but use accepted Euphorbia names.
taxonomy_notes.caution: Do not create duplicate learner cards for legacy Chamaesyce names.

genus_diagnostics.latex: Many Euphorbia release milky latex that may irritate skin/eyes; latex is a supporting group clue, not sufficient by itself nor a reason to tear the plant open for ID.
genus_diagnostics.cyathium: Small flower-like INFLORESCENCE formed by a cup/involucre around highly reduced male flowers (each with one stamen) and a central stalked female flower; often edged with nectar glands and sometimes showy gland appendages. Each cup is a cyathium, not one ordinary five-petaled flower.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: A mature 3-lobed capsule generally holds three seeds (one per compartment) and may eject them at maturity. Fine sculpture, hairs and size are especially helpful in look-alike groups.
genus_diagnostics.showy_parts: In some species the conspicuous white or red structures are bracts, not petals.
genus_diagnostics.shoot_morphology: Some species have showy modified bracts, some have inconspicuous reproductive heads, and many sandmats have opposite leaves and inconspicuous stipules. Not all Euphorbia share the same broad growth form.

shared_traits: tiny cyathia rather than ordinary petaled flowers
bracts, glands, hairs, seed surface, and growth form often matter more than flower color
priority: 1. Look for a true cyathium/cup holding reduced flowers, NOT a conventional 5-petaled corolla; look nearby for a three-lobed capsule.
2. Habit: upright WHITE bracts / colored poinsettia-like upright / green toothed upright / creeping low opposite-leaved sandmat.
3. White-bracted group: relative bract width + pubescence specifically on the UPPER surface, not just hairs on stems.
4. Poinsettia-looking group: greenhouse red pattern is NOT final; close-up must resolve exact gland opening and annular rim.
5. E. dentata vs E. davidii: mature seed and underside hairs are essential; do not make a reliable species call from a capsule-only photograph.
6. Sandmats: check whether each node roots, inspect minute stipules, then capsule keel hair and mature seed sculpture; photograph 2 mm scale.
study_strategy.warning: CAUTION: most local Euphorbia release latex that can irritate skin or eyes; never break stems for students unnecessarily. Several species have overlapping leaf color/habit and even mature flowers. Match photo anatomy first. Texas-native status is species- and COUNTY-dependent, not genus-wide; E. davidii currently retains an unresolved range-label exception until target-county evidence is reconciled.
study_strategy.look_here_first: FIND A CYATHIUM AND A THREE-LOBED CAPSULE before choosing a species. A Euphorbia cyathium is a cup holding tiny reduced male flowers and ONE stalked female flower; it often resembles a single normal flower, but is an INFLORESCENCE. Next sort the plant into four field groups: WHITE showy bracts → bicolor / marginata; upright poinsettia-like bracts → cyathophora / heterophylla; upright green toothed foliage → dentata / davidii; small low opposite-leaved sandmat → examine rooting nodes, stipules, capsule hairs and seed surface. Latex alone or red leaf spots do not prove species.

field_groups.look_here_first: Upper-surface hairiness + width/shape of the white-margined bracts.
differences: E. bicolor: narrow linear to narrowly oblanceolate white-margined bracts; upper leaf/bract surfaces conspicuously hairy.
E. marginata: broader elliptic to obovate white-margined bracts; upper leaf surfaces mostly glabrous.

field_groups.look_here_first: Color at the upper bract base, then inspect the cyathial gland opening.
differences: E. cyathophora: upper bracts often sharply colored red/pink/white at the base; gland opening oblong and lacking an annular rim.
E. heterophylla: upper bracts usually green or merely pale; gland opening circular with an annular rim.

field_groups.look_here_first: Mature seed + capsule size + hair texture beneath the leaves.
differences: E. dentata: smaller capsules/seeds; seeds more rounded in cross section and evenly finely tuberculate; hairs generally longer and less stiff.
E. davidii: larger capsules/seeds; seeds more angular with uneven tubercles/wrinkles; hairs shorter, stiffer, often on minute pustular bases.

field_groups.look_here_first: For the prostrata–serpens–villifera trio, inspect a stem node before judging overall habit: node-rooting + stipule architecture is the fastest split. Then compare pubescence, capsule hairs/cocci, and mature seed sculpture. Use broader habit/leaf characters to separate E. angusta, E. fendleri, and E. nutans.
differences: E. angusta: erect perennial with narrow linear to elliptic-linear distal leaves; stems/involucre/capsule strigose.
E. fendleri: low perennial from a woody crown; clustered glabrous stems, small entire leaves, distinct narrow stipules, glabrous capsule.
E. nutans: larger opposite leaves and ascending/erect branching; reddish leaf blotch often present but not required.
E. prostrata: prostrate/decumbent and not rooting at nodes; upper-side stipules free but lower-side pair fused; capsule keels hairy; seed sharply ridged.
E. serpens: strictly prostrate and frequently rooting at nodes; fused broad-deltate stipule scales; plant and capsule glabrous; seed smooth.
E. villifera: usually erect/ascending; distinct filiform stipules and papillate surfaces; usually villous but sometimes glabrous; capsule glabrous with often elongated empty-tipped cocci.
photo_roles: matched stem-node views showing no rooting vs adventitious roots
matched stipule macros: prostrata upper-free/lower-fused vs serpens fused deltate scale vs villifera filiform
matched capsule macros: prostrata hairy keels vs serpens glabrous vs villifera glabrous elongated cocci
overhead/side habit views as supporting context

quick_key.if: White-margined narrow or broad modified upper leaves/bracts, upright prairie weed
quick_key.then: WHITE PAIR: narrow upper hairy E. bicolor vs broad upper mostly smooth E. marginata — inspect leaf face and bract width.

quick_key.if: Upright green-to-pink/red poinsettia-like leafy tops and tiny cups
quick_key.then: POINTSETTIA PAIR: E. cyathophora vs E. heterophylla — compare gland opening oblong/rimless vs round/rimmed under magnification. If gland unclear, keep pair unresolved.

quick_key.if: Erect branched weed with opposite toothed green leaves and several green 3-lobed capsules
quick_key.then: DENTATA COMPLEX: E. dentata vs E. davidii — collect/photograph mature seed and underside hairs; habit alone DOES NOT separate.

quick_key.if: Creeping flat mat of tiny opposite leaves
quick_key.then: SANDMAT KEY: capsule face hairs maculata, capsule keel hairs prostrata, smooth capsules serpens OR villifera. For smooth-fruited specimens check villifera's typically erect habit, separate threadlike stipules and papillate leaf surfaces versus serpens' prostrate rooted mat and fused triangular stipules; microscopic villifera diagnostics on PHOTO HOLD.

quick_key.if: Plant's leaves/bracts or capsule don't fit these groups
quick_key.then: Stay Euphorbia sp. and check remaining locally documented species; these quick keys cover common groups, not every species in the genus.

diagnostic_review_2026_10_07.note: All 12 canonical learner species now have a detailed morphology/look-alike pass and at least one physical learner image; several retain explicit macro-photo polish targets.

curation_status.photo_note: Original indexed study photos preserved as source references. Public genus panel filters rights and adds only visually confirmed arrows. Species-level galleries retain their own licensing gates.

visual_comparison.title: Euphorbia — begin with habit, then the tiny real reproductive parts
visual_comparison.subtitle: Four-sandmat comparison: maculata capsule face hairs, prostrata keel hairs, serpens smooth fruit + fused stipules, villifera typically ASCENDING with glabrous capsule and threadlike stipules (unresolved at photo level). Villifera's papillae and internally empty fruit tip are not proven by available images.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: Euphorbia = tiny CYATHIUM (not a normal flower) + 3-lobed CAPSULE. First sort WHITE-bracted / POINSETTIA-looking / TOOTHED erect / SANDMAT. Then look at the part that truly separates the two likely species. Colored bracts, red spots and white latex are supporting clues, not final proof.

look_here_first: FIND A CYATHIUM AND A THREE-LOBED CAPSULE before choosing a species. A Euphorbia cyathium is a cup holding tiny reduced male flowers and ONE stalked female flower; it often resembles a single normal flower, but is an INFLORESCENCE. Next sort the plant into four field groups: WHITE showy bracts → bicolor / marginata; upright poinsettia-like bracts → cyathophora / heterophylla; upright green toothed foliage → dentata / davidii; small low opposite-leaved sandmat → examine rooting nodes, stipules, capsule hairs and seed surface. Latex alone or red leaf spots do not prove species.

comparison_cards.title: Snow-on-the-prairie vs snow-on-the-mountain
comparison_cards.look_here_first: FIELD KEY WITH TWO INDEPENDENT CHARACTERS: E. bicolor has long/narrow (linear-narrowly oblanceolate) white-edged bracts PLUS noticeable SOFT HAIRS on the TOP leaf/bract face. E. marginata generally has broader elliptic-obovate bracts PLUS UPPER surfaces smooth/glabrous, even when its STEM and lower midrib are hairy. Bract whiteness or 'patchy versus frosty' is not diagnostic.

comparison_cards.title: Sandmat Euphorbia: FOUR-WAY capsule hairs, stipules and seed key
comparison_cards.look_here_first: FIRST SORT HABIT: villifera usually ascends upright (rarely prostrate), the other three typically creep. Then examine the actual 3-lobed capsule: MACULATA has fine hairs spread across capsule FACES; PROSTRATA shows hairs along raised KEELS; SERPENS is GLABROUS; VILLIFERA is also GLABROUS, so do NOT confuse villifera with serpens on capsule hairs alone. Villifera needs separate FILIFORM stipules + PAPILLATE leaf blades and often elongated empty-tipped capsule cocci (microscopy/dissection required). Seed confirmation: MACULATA weak transverse ribs; PROSTRATA strong transverse ridges; SERPENS smooth; VILLIFERA smooth or faintly rugose/weakly cross-ridged. Photo evidence for villifera stipules, papillae, seed and coccus internal tip is still incomplete.

comparison_cards.title: Erect or ascending spurges: E. nutans vs E. villifera
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Two spurges can rise above the soil and BOTH have a glabrous 3-lobed capsule. FIRST look at LEAF LENGTH AND SHAPE: nutans 8–40 mm oblong leaves, finely toothed edges and strongly unequal bases; villifera smaller 3–12 mm ovate blades. Then check the tiny STIPULES with 10–20×: nutans small FRINGED/DIVIDED SCALES 1–1.5 mm, villifera distinct FILIFORM threads 0.3–0.7 mm. Nutans seed irregular fine wrinkles; villifera seed may be smooth or faintly wrinkled (villifera mature seed macro still missing). Red spots, leaf hairs, upright habit and smooth fruit alone are NOT deciding characters.

comparison_cards.title: Three upright look-alikes: hypericifolia vs nutans vs hyssopifolia
comparison_cards.look_here_first: FIRST SORT THE INFLORESCENCE, NOT BLOTTED LEAVES. Hypericifolia has crowded, almost headlike GLOMERULES of many tiny cyathia with reduced bract leaves; nutans and hyssopifolia usually bear scattered solitary cyathia or smaller more leafy cymes. Next inspect LOWER STEM HAIRS: hypericifolia generally glabrous; nutans with short curved hairs; hyssopifolia variably pilose below but may be hairless distally. Finally, magnify the STIPULES: hypericifolia larger fused triangular scales 1.5–2.2 mm vs hyssopifolia shorter divided scales 0.5–1 mm; nutans irregularly divided/fringed scales. Nutans and hyssopifolia overlap considerably in leaf shape and capsule smoothness. For difficult plants, demand micro photos and ripe seed.

comparison_cards.title: Small round Euphorbia flower heads: ophthalmica vs hirta vs hypericifolia
comparison_cards.look_here_first: FOLLOW THE HAIRY STEM TO THE CYATHIUM HEAD. OPHTHALMICA usually forms low prostrate shoots (6–22 cm) with dense capitate GLOMERULES restricted to the tips of main shoots or very short LEAFY side branches. HIRTA produces terminal AND axillary glomerules, with axillary heads sometimes carried on elongate LEAFLESS stalks, and often taller stems. HYPERICIFOLIA may also have both terminal/axillary rounded heads but is usually GLABROUS with glabrous capsules and fused DELTOID stipules; OPHTHALMICA has visibly hairy leaves and finely hairy capsules. NUTANS usually has single cyathia or smaller loosely clustered leafy cymes and a glabrous capsule. Unmeasured stipule size and leaf redness do NOT identify a plant.
